item.description:
Israeli communities shattered by Hamas masacres are torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relatives

Keith Siegel spent many of his long hours in Hamas captivity in Gaza etching everything that happened after 7 October 2023 into his memory. For 484 days, he recited to himself every place he was held, the dates he was moved and every attack or humiliation he endured or witnessed.

He aimed to store intelligence that could help Israeli forces free other hostages if he was released, to keep track of time as the days slid by and be able to tell his family what happened to him. Now his body is free, but he cannot loosen those memories.

Three years on from the 7 October attacks, antisemitism has taken hold in Britain: Jews aren’t safe | Dave Rich
item.description:
Britain cannot call itself a diverse democracy when communities are living with such fear. A line must be drawn. Let it be now

On another anniversary of the 7 October attacks, the lasting impact on Britain’s Jews is found in the essential daily decisions we now have to make. Beyond the simple fear that you or your children might get killed the next time you go to synagogue or visit your local kosher shop, Jews are hiding the fact they are Jewish.

This has gone beyond the choice of whether to wear your Star of David necklace inside or outside your shirt. It is found in the job applicants who remove their Jewish community volunteering from their CV; the people who use false names when ordering an Uber; the parents who move their children from mainstream schools to Jewish ones.

Dave Rich is director of policy at the Community Security Trust. His new book, From Be’eri to Bondi: Global Antisemitism After October 7, is published by Routledge

item.title: The Greens may yet win in Holborn and St Pancras – but what happened to the party set to ‘replace’ Labour? | Andy Beckett
item.description:
On the eve of the byelection, Polanski’s pledge is to keep the government ‘in check’. It may not be enough to stop a drift back to the political margins

Only a few months ago, in the spring, there was a sense of giddy possibility about the Greens. Zack Polanski’s radical new leadership felt fresh and dynamic, especially compared with those of the other parties. Former Labour supporters, in particular, were switching to the Greens in huge numbers, Green candidates were winning across the country, and the party was second behind Reform UK in some national polls.

Like Reform, the Green party presented itself as a revolt against a failed status quo. Unlike Reform, the Greens’ urgent stance on the climate crisis gave them a potent moral authority: even many people who did not support them believed that the Greens were right about the most universal issue.

item.title: The AI gender gap is about more than women. It’s about a broken system
item.description:
When I was designing the cover of my book, Ambitious Mother, I tried to get a little help from artificial intelligence. We had worked hard on the visuals with the design team, and after many drafts I just wanted to see what a different color font would look like, without asking them for more changes. I put the photo into AI and prompted it to show me the exact same cover, but with green text instead of red.

Imagine my surprise when the image that came back was the same cover, in the new color, but instead of Ambitious Mother, the book had been renamed Ambitious Father. And the author’s name had changed from Anne Welsh to John Welsh.

I was shocked and also not.

On one hand, I had a healthy skepticism of AI. We knew it would “hallucinate” articles. I knew to constantly double-check the research, the numbers, the citations, and more. I did that diligently. 

At the same time, I had made a very simple request and the response felt like much more than a mistake. It felt like a statement: AI was SO unfamiliar with the idea of these two words being placed next to each other, it had to make it a new set of words to finish the prompt. And then changed the author’s gender to match.

We have an assumption that computers are not biased because they are based on data and therefore somehow objective. And yet, AI is trained on what already exists, and what exists is biased. Whose stories are told in the history books? Whose stories are represented in the data? Who do we study and how to do we interpret that data? 

The real danger is that people don’t always know what bias is baked in, and we aren’t always asking the right questions.

An Old Double Bind, Dressed up in New Tech

I’ve been thinking about that story again as we talk more and more about the gender gap in AI use. More often than not, we talk about gender gaps in leadership as if they are a woman’s problem to solve. We tell women: Speak up. Be more confident. Negotiate. Advocate for yourself.

The problem with this advice is that behaviors are not treated the same in men and women.

We have known this for a long time although we don’t always talk about it. For example, research on the leadership double bind has found that women need to demonstrate the strength associated with effective leadership while also demonstrating the warmth we expect from women. Women who are assertive enough to be seen as competent can then be penalized for not being warm or likable enough. 

I see this play out with my clients in many ways. One client was an attending at a major health center. At multiple points in her training she watched male colleagues receive praise for their amazing bedside manner when they asked a simple question that involved any degree of empathy. Meanwhile, female colleagues consistently demonstrated empathy and excellent bedside manner, and it was simply expected. In contrast, when women veer from that expectation, they receive sharp criticism, while men are exempt. 

Now I see us doing a version of the same thing with AI.

What the Research Shows

There is an AI gender gap. According to recent research from Lean In, men are 22% more likely than women to say they use AI daily or constantly at work. This is important to notice and fix. AI is going to be part of how we work, and addressing this is important.

But we keep talking about the gap as though the solution is simply getting women to use AI more. That ignores the environment in which we are asking them to adopt it.

In the same Lean In research, men were 23% more likely than women to say their managers encouraged them to use AI, and 27% more likely to say they had been praised for using it. Meanwhile, women were 32% more likely to worry that using AI would be perceived as cheating.

And women may be correctly assessing the situation as more fraught for them.

In a recent study of more than 1,000 software engineers, researchers had participants evaluate identical code while changing whether they were told it had been produced with AI and whether the engineer was a man or a woman. When people thought AI had been used, everyone took a competence hit. But women took a bigger one. The competence penalty for women was more than twice the penalty for men.

In this study, the work didn’t change. What changed was the evaluator’s knowledge that AI had helped produce it. And while everyone took a hit to perceived competence, it was significantly different for men and women.

In a follow-up survey in the same paper, researchers also found that people who anticipated a greater competence penalty were slower to adopt AI, and that relationship was stronger among women.

Essentially, women accurately perceive that they will be judged more for using AI and are therefore less likely to adopt it. And this is where everything feels familiar. Women are told just do X, without the context that X is perceived differently for men and women. 

Women were told to negotiate more. Later research found that women were asking for raises and promotions as often as men but were less likely to get them, while other studies have found that women can be penalized for initiating negotiations. 

And now we’re saying: Just use AI. Women need to learn it. They need to catch up.

But when they do, they may be perceived differently.

We also have to address the issue of invisible labor and the leisure gap here. Women have less discretionary time. OECD data have consistently found that women spend more time on unpaid work and less time on leisure than men. This means that outside work, they simply have less time to address the steep learning curve that high-level AI use requires. 

There are also differences in how we value the time that women do put into AI learning. In the women’s leadership groups that I lead, I have heard from multiple women who are taking on AI adoption roles in their organizations without having that work compensated or even really named as work. They are asked to be on the AI committee, to help other people figure it out, or to think through some of the ethical and people questions around AI. And in multiple cases, I have watched those roles become more formalized only to have the formal roles go to men.

I’ve written before about the problem of invisible labor at work, so I won’t rehash it here. But I do think we have to ask a basic question: If women are spending their time doing the invisible work of AI adoption for everyone else, or doing all of the other invisible work that still disproportionately falls to women, when exactly are they supposed to find the extra time to learn and experiment on their own? And why aren’t we giving them credit for any of it? 

Baked-in Bias

And then we come back to the technology itself.

Circling back to the idea of warmth and competence we started with, we see the same perception reiterated by technology. Researchers compared human and AI-generated judgments using the classic dimensions of warmth and competence. In ChatGPT-generated ratings, women were portrayed as warmer and less competent than men. Even more strikingly, the gender differences were larger in the AI-generated ratings and images than in the comparable human-generated material. 

And that cover swap I told you about? In a 2026 study out of Germany, researchers generated 1,344 images with various prompts. When the prompt was to generate an image of “a person” or “a warm person” the AI was more likely to show women. When the prompt was “a competent person” the image was more likely to be a man. 

This shows up in specific work contexts too. A 2025 study published in Nature asked ChatGPT to generate fictional résumés across 54 occupations. When the applicant had a woman’s name, ChatGPT generated applicants who were younger, had graduated more recently, and had less relevant experience than when the applicant had a man’s name.

That doesn’t mean AI is going to take your résumé and suddenly erase years of your experience, but it does show that we cannot assume objectivity simply because the information came from a computer. AI makes assumptions about women’s competence and experience based on baked-in bias. We have to work against that in our workplaces and in our own use of AI. 

What Companies Can Do

As with all things, there are individual and systemic contributions and solutions here. And once again, we are taking a systemic issue and offering only individual solutions: Women just need to catch up with AI.

Instead, we need to see both/and.

Yes, women need the skills to use AI and we need to address this gap. But, we need to address the gap by addressing the bias, not just the women. We can think about it in four categories: 

1. Encouragement

Organizations need to question how they approach AI and ask themselves: Who are you encouraging to use AI? Who has access to the tools and the training? Who are you praising when they do? Who is doing the work of AI adoption, and who eventually gets recognized as the expert?

2. Time

Learning any new tool takes time. Time to play, to make mistakes, to experiment. If AI is important, then make sure the women also have time to learn it. It cannot be left to “spare time” because we know that women have less of that.

3. Visibility

If someone is spending time on AI work for your organization—teaching, evaluating, learning—make sure that it all counts. Name it, include it in promotion conversations, and make sure they get credit even before it’s formalized.

4. Evaluation

We need to pay attention to how we evaluate work. Standardize what constitutes appropriate AI use and how the finished product gets evaluated. If knowing that someone used AI changes how competent you think they are, would you make the same judgment if the person doing the work were someone else?

Of course, we also need to bring that same scrutiny to the AI tools themselves, particularly when they are being used to make decisions about people. If AI is helping screen candidates, summarize performance feedback, or make recommendations about talent, we cannot assume that its output is objective simply because a computer produced it. The emerging research on gender, warmth, competence, and experience gives us good reason to keep asking questions.

If we want women to adopt AI at the same rate as men, we have to address the differences in time, opportunity, perception, judgment, and recognition that make adoption a different proposition for women in the first place.

Otherwise, we’re once again identifying a gender gap and telling women to fix it.

item.title: Why AI’s easiest wins are misleading CEOs
Young workers are turning toward AI-proof jobs
item.description:
Entry level jobs are an endangered animal, at least in professions exposed to disruption from AI. While new grads are still seeing opportunities in fields like real estate, utilities and construction, the overall hiring market has been brutal: a whopping 48% of recent college graduates were unemployed (5.6%) or underemployed (42%) and working in jobs that didn’t require a degree in the second quarter of 2026. 

Indeed, an analysis from Stanford Digital Economy Lab finds young people may be gravitating toward “AI-proof” jobs involving physical labor, social interaction, and other skills that are harder to automate. The researchers drew upon ADP administrative payroll data covering millions of U.S. workers to examine what has happened to employment since generative AI became widely available.

In professions with high exposure to AI like customer service and software engineering, employment among workers ages 22 to 25 is 19% lower than it would be if it had kept pace with employment among the same age group in other professions since 2022, the research shows.

While employment of workers aged 22 to 25 fell by about 11% in the 40% of jobs that were most exposed to AI, it rose about 10% in other, less AI-exposed job categories. The gap for younger workers has widened considerably since last August, when the researchers identified a 13% divergence. Slower hiring, rather than increased “separations,” has driven the lower headcount among recent graduates, which is concentrated in professions where AI automates human tasks rather than complements them.

The apparent trend is also limited to younger workers; the study found no evidence of “widespread, economy-wide job displacement” associated with AI. For experienced workers, there was no gap whatsoever between more AI-exposed and less AI-exposed roles.

The findings are the latest evidence that AI is transforming early-career knowledge work, eliminating jobs and creating anxiety among younger workers. According to the Pew Research Center, the percentage of people under 30 who believe AI will lead to fewer jobs rose 12% in two years, to 73%.

The technology is also changing expectations for junior workers who do land entry level jobs in fields impacted by AI. According to a study by PwC, junior hires at such jobs are seven times more likely to require mid-career capabilities such as leadership and strategic thinking.

Along with job security, higher education costs, and other issues, AI may be contributing to increased Gen Z interest in skilled trades like construction and plumbing.

On a balmy, quiet evening in June 2020, Otto’s elderly mother, Doria, was fading in her Munich apartment. As she lay with her eyes closed, her pale face, framed by her white hair, was calm.

Otto, masked, gloved and draped in a sterile apron, dozed in a chair beside her. Otto, who sometimes goes by the name Rainer, and whose last name is only known as “Z” because of Germany’s strict privacy laws, was a doctor who had cared for his mother for years, ever since she had suffered a stroke and moved in with him. He described the course of that night to me. He woke to the sound of her short breath and tried to sit her upright. Her eyes were shut, and her lips pursed. She stopped breathing. Otto reached for his phone to call for help, but then Doria opened her eyes and stared into his. She smiled, drew one last deep breath, shut her eyes again, and lay still.

The Norwegian government has given a permit to a mining company to release waste into Førde fjord despite a 17-year battle by campaigners and a supreme court ruling against it

Shortly after the Norwegian stock market closed on 17 June 2026, a few dozen local people from the small west coast town of Vevring crowded around a laptop in a school. Surrounded by children’s drawings and windows looking out over Førde fjord, they listened as news arrived from Oslo. Norway’s supreme court had ruled against its government: a permit to release mining waste directly into the fjord two miles upstream was illegal, the court said.

The moment marked the end of a 17-year fight, one of Norway’s most protracted environmental battles in living memory. In Oslo, Ingvild Fonn Asmervik, the project leader for Naturvernforbundet (Friends of the Earth Norway), compared the joy she felt to giving birth to her child. For Anne-Line Thingnes Førsund, a third-generation fisher living on the banks of the fjord in Vevring and a volunteer for the charity’s local branch, it was more of a relief. Like a mountain lifting off her shoulders, she said.

item.description:
The combination of Iranian, Russian and Chinese aggression is deeply worrying: just how much more concerned about security should the country be?

The first time the window-rattling roar of a B-1 bomber woke me up this summer, I thought for one crazed second we were under attack. By the second time, I’d learned to recognise the sound of US planes taking off from their base at RAF Fairford for what it was: a reminder that although Britain wants no part in this war with Iran, we cannot quite escape the consequences.

We’ll feel them at the petrol pump, or in the supermarket this autumn, or in this winter’s heating bills. But living under the flight path adds an extra edge to it. The skies finally fell silent last week, but only because the bombers have been hastily summoned home after an alleged terrorist plot to attack Fairford, in which (according to the prime minister) there are “strong indications that Iran played a part”. If Fairford is now a target of war, did that threat disappear when the Americans did? Nobody knows.

item.title: The Guardian view on Ethiopia’s return to conflict: civilian catastrophe and a spiralling regional polycrisis | Editorial
item.description:
The escalating violence reflects deep domestic rifts – but is fuelled by broader geopolitical power games

When the Nobel peace laureate is announced on Friday, the committee will be hoping that its choice ages better than 2019’s. Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, won the prize for ending the 20-year border conflict with neighbouring Eritrea – signing a peace agreement with President Isaias Afwerki. A year later, their new relationship facilitated a war with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) that killed as many as 600,000 people, displaced millions more, led to atrocities by both sides, and pushed Tigrayans into famine.

Both sides bear responsibility for failing to properly implement the deal that ended that conflict in 2022, and the African Union and US did little to ensure that a piece of paper became a durable settlement. Now violence has resurged in northern Ethiopia, and old foes are forming bizarre new pacts. Last month, seven Ethiopian regional groups announced an “Alliance for Survival” to remove the federal government. Mr Abiy’s coalition is held together by his patronage, but so far may be faring better than his rivals, united solely by shared loathing of him and riven by deep disputes. The TPLF, which controls Tigray, has previously battled the Fano militia of Amhara, and their territorial dispute endures. Ethiopia accuses Eritrea – previously accused of atrocities against Tigrayan civilians – of backing the rebel alliance. Despite Asmara’s denials, there are multiple reports of Eritrean troops in Tigray.

  • Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

In the field of global health, we often talk about each generation living longer and healthier lives than their parents. We’ve seen this in the gains in life expectancy, the sharp decrease in child mortality and in the near elimination of many vaccine-preventable diseases. But since the turn of the century this progress has stalled, and in some cases several health metrics have gone backwards.

Take cancer, which was long thought to be a disease linked to old age. While most cancers do indeed still occur in elderly people, a new report highlights that a number of cancers are increasing in people who are under 50, often referred to as “early onset cancer”. The report, undertaken by the World Cancer Research Fund, looked at data from 12 different cancer types in England, the US and the Netherlands over the past 20 years. What they found isn’t pretty.

item.title: How do human beings rationalize genocide? NAZA provides a chilling look | Omer Bartov
item.description:
It’s easier to blame brutes and sadists for extreme violence. But as we see in the documentary, modern genocides are fueled by people who are uncomfortably recognizable

Werner Best, a senior SS official and jurist who helped organize the Nazi death squads that murdered hundreds of thousands of Jews, is also known for his statement: “We must destroy the enemy without hating him.” He belonged to a younger generation of Nazi technocrats, who despised the foul-mouthed, beer-bellied, brown-shirted “old fighters” of the Nazi party in the 1920s, and believed in organizing genocide neatly and dispassionately. After the fall of the regime, Best escaped justice for the rest of his long life, dying peacefully in Germany in 1989. His chilling statement came to my mind while I was watching the film NAZA.

I grew up in Tel Aviv and have visited there often in recent years. That is why the interviews with 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers, which make up this documentary, felt strangely familiar. The conversations are conducted at night on rooftops, and the camera scans the cityscape, lingering on apartment windows as their inhabitants watch TV and make dinner. The landscape was intimately recognizable, and I felt a natural affinity with those people living their lives. I also recognized the way the interviewees talked – their speech patterns and choice of words. They reminded me of my son, who served more than a decade ago in the intelligence unit many of them might have belonged to.

item.title: Googlebooks mark the end of the old Google
item.description:
Does Google still believe in the open web? With the launch of its new Googlebooks, it doesn’t feel that way.

Googlebooks are Google’s attempt to establish a new platform of Android-based laptops, with native Android app support and tight connectivity with Android phones. They’re also an extension of Google’s efforts to rebuild Android around AI, with Gemini features just a quick cursor gesture away.

At the same time, Google plans to phase out ChromeOS, which it introduced in 2009 as a lightweight platform for the web. While Chromebooks remain popular in the education sector, Google says it will convert many existing models to Googlebooks, and it will end support for ChromeOS entirely by 2034.

it’s a sad end for what once represented Google at its most idealistic. Chromebooks weren’t just a breakthrough in speed and simplicity for laptops, they were also a bold bet on the open web as the next great computing platform. As the web becomes more walled off, and Google pivots to a platform more directly under its control, that dream has finally run its course.

How Chromebooks lost their way

The original goal for Chrome OS was to strip away all the overhead of a traditional laptop to make computing faster and easier. Here’s what Google wrote about the project in 2009:

“Speed, simplicity and security are the key aspects of Google Chrome OS. We’re designing the OS to be fast and lightweight, to start up and get you onto the web in a few seconds. The user interface is minimal to stay out of your way, and most of the user experience takes place on the web. And as we did for the Google Chrome browser, we are going back to the basics and completely redesigning the underlying security architecture of the OS so that users don’t have to deal with viruses, malware and security updates. It should just work.”

The first Chromebooks, which arrived in 2011, were basically just laptops that ran the Chrome browser, plus some extra window dressing. They had minimal internal storage and couldn’t run regular desktop software, but this allowed them to stay nimble, with speedy boot times, frictionless software updates, and minimal risk of malware. If a user lost their Chromebook, they could simply set up a new one and pick up where they left off.

In essence, Google was betting that nearly everything people did with their laptops would happen in a browser through sites like Gmail and Google Docs, so they could cut out all the other bloat to make those web apps shine.

To that end, Google encouraged app makers to build for the open web, with applications that could run in any browser, Chromebooks included. Although Google maintained a “Chrome Web Store” for web apps and extensions, the platform was only limited by the web itself. Anything you could run in a browser, you could run on a Chromebook, and that benefitted Google because it meant more people were using its search engine to find things.

“[A]ny time our users have a better computing experience [with Chrome OS], Google benefits as well by having happier users who are more likely to spend time on the Internet,” the company wrote in its 2008 blog post.

Over time, Google wavered on that original vision. It brought Android apps to Chrome OS in 2016, then added support for Linux apps in 2018. It even made a big foray into installable high-end gaming with Steam support.

While these inclusions made Chromebooks more capable, they also added new layers of complexity and demanded laptops with more storage. Setting up a new Chromebook became more of an ordeal, and preserving security became a bigger challenge. In shifting away from laptops powered by the open web, Chrome OS became exactly the kind of heavyweight computing experience it was trying to replace.

All this helped open the door for a new operating system built on Android instead. While Googlebooks will include a desktop-class version of Chrome, the emphasis now is on running Android apps and using AI.

Meanwhile, the original tenets of ChromeOS have disappeared. Look through Google’s announcement post for Googlebooks, and you will not find the words “speed,” “simplicity,” or “security” mentioned even once.

Times have changed, and so has Google

Google’s pivot away from a web-based operating system shouldn’t come as a major surprise. After all, Googlebooks are arriving at a time when the open web is destabilizing, in part because of Google itself.

Along with other tech companies that are all-in on AI, Google is betting on a world where browsing the web is increasingly unnecessary. Instead of using Google Search as a gateway to other sites, Google intends to have AI generate whatever information you need. Instead of managing your own email inbox, chatbots like Gemini will manage it for you. Instead of visiting websites to shop or make restaurant reservations, AI companies want to deploy fleets of AI agents to navigate those sites on your behalf.

As a result, using the web as a human is becoming more difficult. A growing number of websites are blocking themselves off from search engines and archival services in an attempt to keep AI crawlers out. Amazon has been limiting how many customer reviews some users can read because it thinks their behavior looks too robotic. Even just proving that you’re not a bot requires increasingly complicated steps, as in Google’s new ReCAPTCHA systems that demand phone-based verification or a recording of yourself performing hand gestures.

It’d be wrong to say that Google’s strategy with Chromebooks had anything to do with this. The company faltered on its original vision for a variety of other reasons, and the rise of AI would have been inevitable anyway.

Still, the arrival of Googlebooks serves as one final reminder of what we’ve lost. There was a time when Google believed in the open web more than anything, and it was committed to a platform with no real boundaries.

But that was back when getting folks to spend more time on the web was Google’s ultimate goal. Googlebooks exist for a world in which Google is clawing back more of that time for itself.

item.title: The more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support Ukraine | Timothy Garton Ash
item.description:
Moscow’s imperialist strongman believes decadent European democracies can be cowed. Our job is to prove him wrong

Vladimir Putin is escalating both his full-scale war against Ukraine and his shadow war against the rest of Europe. His main purpose in the shadow one is to break European support for Ukraine so he can subjugate that country, something he regards as existential for Russia’s future and his own. While we in the rest of Europe must prepare as best we can to defend ourselves against every kind of hybrid attack, the central thrust of our response should be to redouble our support for Ukraine. Ukraine is his main target. It’s there, and only there, not in a contest of a thousand hybrid pinpricks, that Putin’s Russia can in a meaningful sense be defeated and deterred.

In a powerful new book, Warum Russland nicht aufhören wird (Why Russia Won’t Stop), the German historian Martin Schulze Wessel shows how Putin’s policy fits into a much older Russian tradition of territorial expansionism and striving for hegemony, combined with a religiously infused imperial ideology. He reminds us that in 2016 Putin said “Russia’s frontier ends nowhere” and in 2025, “wherever the boot of a Russian soldier steps, that is ours”. West Europeans, fondly imagining that we have consigned such brute territorial imperialism to the dustbin of history, tend to think there must be some other explanation (eg something we did “wrong”, like the eastward expansion of Nato). Finns, Estonians and Poles know better. Despite Russia’s weaknesses, the author concludes, it is “the most dangerous country in the world”. Some in Asia might question that large claim, but certainly Russia is the most dangerous country for Europe.

In the Peterloo massacre of 1819, peaceful protesters were shot and trampled to death by the Manchester and Salford Yeomanry at St Peter’s Field in the city.

A study by Global Threads, a public history project, has examined how the exploitation of Africans enslaved in the Caribbean was linked with the struggles of cotton workers at Peterloo. item.title: In three years, Israel's war on Gaza hasn't just changed the Middle East, it's changed the world | Steve Bloomfield
item.description:
A whirlpool of violence has engulfed everywhere from Lebanon to Yemen. Meanwhile, the west has destroyed any political authority it once had

There was a world before 7 October, 2023, and now there is a world after. For Gaza, for Israel, for the wider Middle East, and for everyone else too. Not all hinge points in history are obvious at the time. Three years on from the day it began, and precisely one year since a supposed ceasefire was agreed, this one is now impossible to ignore.

The before-and-after pictures tell part of the story. An update to Google Maps, released last week, underscores just what three years of relentless Israeli military onslaught has done to Gaza. Satellite images show how entire towns have been reduced to rubble. Mosques and hospitals, visible three years ago, have now disappeared. Meanwhile the once-empty shoreline is now crammed with tents. This is what it looks like when an attempt has been made to destroy a people.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

On Saturday I went to Liverpool with my youngest, and the overhead lines went down at Crewe, but also there were crew shortages across the land, so between the homophones and my lifelong inability to start listening to a train announcement until halfway through, I cannot tell you at what point this journey became a five-train, four-hour odyssey. All I know is what’s happening on every train, in every part of the country. The 7.48am is a calm and ordered cohort of people who think they know where they’re going and will be there soon. And from 9.04am onwards, everyone’s drunk, all the way to everywhere.

Between Rugby and Birmingham New Street, there was an incredibly festive crowd going to the Horse of the Year show, squishing real fruit into cans of Pimm’s, because it was breakfast time, and also because it was funny. But what were the horses going to make of all this? Because they’re quite short on appreciation for ludic pranking, and famously easy to frighten.

item.title: How to escape our collective paralysis in ‘these uncertain times’
item.description:
Author Natasha Lennard discusses how to disrupt the ‘certainties’ that don’t serve us and how to fight back

At the onset of the Covid pandemic in 2020, journalist Natasha Lennard started noticing a constant thrum of collective apprehension, epitomized in the phrase “in these uncertain times”. The expression acknowledged we didn’t have solutions for many of society’s problems: a globally spreading virus, the rise of the far right and stark “haves v have-nots” inequalities. In the years since, that “uncertainty” hasn’t gone anywhere, risking enabling paralysis – not knowing where to start to fix things and therefore giving up before trying.

In her new book, On Un/Certainty: The Uses of Doubt in Dangerous Times, Lennard, who also was an organizer in the 2011 Occupy Wall Street movement, deconstructs the problematic nature of giving in to uncertainty. She also uses the Austrian-British philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein’s 1969 book On Certainty to question what is held as “certain” in today’s world, and who gets to make those calls.

• How to make your leather last a lifetime

Take a look at the outfit you’re wearing now: how many times have you worn each item? And how long have you had them? Just over 10 years ago, Eco-Age founder Livia Firth and journalist Lucy Siegle launched the 30 wears challenge to encourage people to buy clothes they would wear at least 30 times.

The 30 wears challenge is a great concept. As a journalist interested in sustainable fashion, I’ve enjoyed applying this rule for years and found the goal can often be surpassed, but with one proviso: clothing must be chosen carefully. The goal is only realistic if garments are of good enough quality to stand up to repeated wear. So, how do you know if your clothes really are well made? Does it mean you have to spend a fortune on them? Do you need to know the difference between a French seam and an overlock seam? And how can we judge clothing quality before buying if we are, like 37% of Britons, getting most of our clothes online? I spoke to experts to find out.

item.title: I was kidnapped and held hostage for 977 days. Could I forgive my captors?
item.description:
At first the idea of mercy was something that helped me through the ordeal. But would real forgiveness be a form of Stockholm syndrome?

I knew Mohamed Tahlil as a gentle pirate who oversaw a team of guards during the first months of my life as a hostage in 2012. I had travelled to Somalia to report on the outbreak of modern piracy off the coast. On the 10th day, along a dusty road near Galkayo, in the centre of the country, I was kidnapped by pirates. For the next two and a half years, I was a hostage.

I spent most of my time on a thin, sweat-soaked foam mattress on the floor of a dusty room. The dim concrete prison houses changed, but the filth and the circumstances didn’t. Sometimes my captors moved me into the Somali savannah – where we camped in the open and slept on the ground – and for a six-month stretch, I was held on a hijacked tuna vessel, where I joined 28 fishers from east Asia who had been captured about three weeks before I was placed on board. (They had captured me on land, but they were a pirate gang, organised to capture ships at sea.) In each location, pirate guards would sit around with AK-47s and listen to the radio, or else chew khat, a narcotic plant.

item.title: Europe’s big election season is about to kick off. It could change everything | Nathalie Tocci
item.description:
If far right nationalists gain power in four big countries simultaneously, we are in for a dramatic Trumpian tilt

When it comes to Europe’s economy or its peace and security, it is obvious that decision-making has to be done largely at the European level to be meaningful. Yet electoral politics is still conducted mostly at the national level. The silver lining of this mismatch is that from country to country in Europe we have governments with different political priorities and leanings. Unlike in the US, where one presidential election can radically change the entire country’s course, as we have seen so vividly under Donald Trump’s leadership, the same drama has not so far unfolded in Europe. This may be about to change.

Pedro Sánchez rolled the dice in Spain last week, calling a snap election for next month after an unholy alliance of the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and Catalan pro-independence party Junts blocked his big housing reform package in parliament. If the socialist prime minister, hailed by progressives globally but demonised by Europe’s right and Trump’s US, loses his election gamble, Spain could fall into the hands of a conservative/far-right coalition, which is currently ahead in the polls.

item.description:
From the FBI to local police departments, US authorities are increasingly warning of would-be terrorists using chatbots to plan attacks and anti-AI extremist threats

In May 2025, a 25-year-old man detonated a car bomb outside a Palm Springs fertility clinic, killing himself and injuring four others. For many, it was a wake-up call about the threats to reproductive care facilities. For the FBI, though, it was also a sign of what the agency had feared for years: bad actors were using generative AI to plan and execute terror plots.

The suspect used an unnamed generative AI tool that failed to detect his request for bomb-making instructions, law enforcement officers wrote in a previously unreported document reviewed by the Guardian. The privacy of his conversation with the AI chatbot hindered alerting police that someone was looking up how to make a bomb, according to the memo.

item.title: Former ARPA-H director Renee Wegrzyn wants to solve science’s ‘magic hands’ problem
item.description:
Renee Wegrzyn spent her career building the future of American science—including the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, or ARPA-H, the White House agency created to accelerate health breakthroughs.

Then the Trump administration showed her the door. Wegrzyn cofounded Transfyr to tackle what she calls one of the most overlooked issues in science: the magic hands problem. She explains why fixing this unglamorous bottleneck is the prerequisite for everything AI promises to deliver in medicine, and why she can feel the next Sputnik moment coming—even if she can’t quite name it yet.

This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, hosted by Robert Safian, former editor-in-chief of Fast Company. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode.

You were at ARPA-H, the inaugural director of a White House effort to accelerate health research. You were amped up about the possibilities, but with the Trump administration, you had to pivot. Was it hard not to take it personally that they wanted different leadership?

I’ll tell you, I’m still amped up about it. It’s still an amazing idea. Obviously, DARPA [the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency] has been around for almost 80 years. I hope ARPA-H will have the same longevity and continue to live on today.

I’m a builder. I love to take things forward and really show what’s possible. So was it hard when I left? Of course it was hard. I had a really unusual appointment: I was a presidential appointee, but I was term-limited, so I served through the transition and had a few weeks in the new administration. I served in “Trump one,” by the way, as well.

So it was a great opportunity to make sure they really understood why we built the agency. We needed an ARPA-H because there was something missing in the way we were doing science broadly, which was: How do you move really quickly? How do you get focused on a problem versus building a general knowledge set? I was able to show them what we were building and convince them that it was worth keeping around. I couldn’t be more proud of the agency and its perseverance.

So your new business, Transfyr—The New York Times wrote about you, and the article kept referring to “magic hands.” I’m curious what magic hands are. What problem is Transfyr trying to solve or address?

You probably have your favorite dish, or your parents’ or grandparents’ favorite dish. Sometimes they just have the magic hands. Nobody can cook it like they do. Nobody can make it taste the special way they can. And that happens in science as well. There are some scientists who just have the knack and can deliver really great science over and over.

The challenge is that a lot of those scientists are such experts they can hardly describe what they’re doing. It’s an art in some ways. And so the magic hands idea was really a testament to what those scientists can do in the lab.

The pipeline we’re creating at Transfyr is: Can we create computer vision and perception tools to capture the work of science as it’s being done so that we understand, if the protocol says, “Mix the cells,” whether someone is inverting the tube in a certain gentle way, while another researcher may be rigorously shaking or vortexing it, which could destroy the sample?

Those little things, compounded over the many decisions a scientist may make over the course of several hours of experimentation, lead to what is called magic hands.

Was this an issue you saw at ARPA-H, the sort of breakthroughs that were trapped in a single lab in some ways?

Where that manifested at DARPA and at ARPA-H was in a realization, through my career, of how fragile breakthroughs are. Usually, the way a breakthrough is first communicated to the world is through a research publication, a Science or Nature paper. That paper is not a product. It’s not commercializable. It’s not ready for a patient that day. That’s the starting gun for what is going to happen.

The ARPAs of this world are really fantastic at getting to that initial breakthrough and demonstrating what is possible, but following through and delivering is not a 100% guaranteed activity.

When I started ARPA-H, we wanted customers, who would be the final users of that technology, to give us feedback on what we were developing so that when we got to the last day of the experiment, they were demanding that product, versus having that be the first contact with a customer, which unfortunately is pretty common around traditional grant-making organizations.

It’s rethinking how you make sure you can transfer that knowledge off the back end of a program.

Because the folks at the lab aren’t necessarily worrying about, or prioritizing, how to make it scalable. They’re just trying to see if it works. But of course, eventually we want it to be scalable.

Sometimes the folks in the lab don’t even have the expertise or understanding of who they need to talk to next to do that, right? We think about science and those transfers as handoffs. We deploy our technology to an originating lab to understand the science and what was important about that discovery, but we can also deploy it in a receiving lab so that we can see how they’re reproducing it.

And instead of the way we transfer science today, which is looking over each other’s shoulders and saying, “Oh, you’re doing it a little wrong,” we have this video-connectedness that lets us help accelerate those iterations of transferring the science.

Do you ever get frustrated about how resources are allocated in our world? You’ve put your life toward this work, and yet so much money is devoted to, I don’t know, space exploration or the next hot social app, the Meta Muse craze. How do you deal with government and how it prioritizes things?

Yeah, it’s maddening. One of the things that has me nervous right now is that I look back on the last 80 years following the Second World War. We’ve led the globe in science and engineering and innovation. Nobody who’s practicing science today has practiced science in the United States at a time when we weren’t, quote-unquote, winning from a competitiveness perspective, when we weren’t at the top.

I genuinely believe we may lose that competitiveness, that edge, that incumbency, and I’m not sure I see us fighting for it in the way that we should be. We have to deliver on what we’ve promised to do, and that’s a commitment not just to my country, but to my kids and my family. 

What I think a lot about is Sputnik moments. We’re going to look back at this moment in time like there’s something happening, and it’s going to impact whatever’s happening 20 to 50 years from now. You can feel it in the moment.

Where that happened before, of course, was Sputnik. The United States didn’t know the Soviet Union was developing that capability, and we didn’t have a counter-capability. What I realized is that each individual person has a Sputnik moment in their life that is usually health-related. My Sputnik moment was when my mother was diagnosed with cancer. That stopped everything.

Everybody has a story, whether it happened to them or their family, or if you talk to a member of Congress, something’s happening in their state that they can’t deal with.

So I’m like, “What is the Sputnik moment now?” If ARPA-H was bringing people from an unhealthy state to a healthy state, what’s happening now is taking us beyond that. If we can figure out and solve health and wellness, a lot of people talk about abundance. What is the next trajectory? What is the Sputnik that we’re working toward?
